new.title: Taste the house beers at Café Bar le Duc
new.desc: Bar le Duc has been a family business since 1975 and is a speciality beer café in the heart of the city. More than a hundred beers are on the list, including a range from the family's own brewery, and the kitchen serves lunch and dinner alongside.
new.tip: Ask about the beer tasting in the brewery's own tasting room, which needs booking. Otherwise let the bar staff pick a house beer for you.

new.title: Choose a table on the Korte Putstraat
new.desc: The Korte Putstraat is a short lane near the cathedral that is known as the restaurant street of Den Bosch. 7evenden Hemel at numbers 13 to 17 is popular with locals and often crowded.
new.tip: Reserve for Friday and Saturday evenings. On other nights, walk the lane once and read the menus before you sit down.

new.title: Have coffee by the old city wall at Het Bolwerk
new.desc: Brasserie Het Bolwerk sits in the old fortification by the former Koepoort, and a stretch of the old city wall stands inside the dining room. Its large sunny terrace lies directly on the Dommel, where small boats come and go.
new.tip: Order a Bossche bol with your coffee at the long reading table. The brasserie may shut for part of the winter, so check that it is open before you set out in the cold months.

new.title: Pair dinner with a film at the Verkadefabriek
new.desc: The Verkade biscuit factory of 1929 on the Boschdijkstraat reopened in 2004 as a cultural centre. Under one roof are two theatre halls, five film screens and a café-restaurant, which makes it an easy evening out.
new.tip: Book a table before your screening on busy nights. Check the programme first, as it mixes film with theatre, cabaret and dance.

new.title: Greet the golden dragon outside the station
new.desc: The Drakenfontein of 1903 is the best known fountain in the city, topped by a gilded dragon. It was paid for from a bequest of 10,000 guilders by the provincial governor Bosch van Drakestein, in memory of his twin daughters, who both died in 1881 at the age of seventeen.
new.tip: It stands just east of the station on the way into town, so you pass it anyway. It was meant as a drinking fountain but never worked as one.

new.title: Meet three generations of painters at Museum Slager
new.desc: Behind old house fronts on the Choorstraat, a short walk from the Sint-Jan, hangs the work of eight painters from one Bosch family. Piet Slager senior founded the dynasty, his children and their spouses followed, and grandson Tom was the last; the museum opened in 1976.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and opens only in the afternoon on Sundays.

new.title: Listen for the Hemony bells of the Stadhuis
new.desc: The city government has sat on this spot on the Markt since 1366, though the classical front you see dates from 1670. In the little tower hangs a carillon cast by the Hemony brothers in 1649 and installed in 1657, which was enlarged to three octaves in 1951.
new.tip: Stand in the middle of the Markt to hear the bells. The medieval cellars under the building house a restaurant.

new.title: Follow the music at Jazz in Duketown
new.desc: Every Whitsun weekend the old town turns into a free open-air jazz festival, run by volunteers since its start on the Markt in 1962. Around ten stages host some eighty concerts, from straight jazz to soul, blues, funk and world music.
new.tip: Everything is free, so drift from square to square instead of planning. Expect crowds: well over a hundred thousand people come over the weekend.

new.title: Catch a show at Theaterfestival Boulevard
new.desc: Each August the Parade, the square at the foot of the Sint-Jan, becomes the heart of the largest theatre festival in the south of the Netherlands. Boulevard has run since 1985, mixing theatre, dance, music and street acts on the square with performances on location in and around the city.
new.tip: The festival square with its small shows and food stalls is the place to start. Book the bigger performances ahead.

new.title: Walk around the IJzeren Vrouw
new.desc: When the city was allowed to grow beyond its walls, sand for the new Muntel district was dug here, leaving a lake up to 24 metres deep. It was named after the dredger, echoing the IJzeren Man in Vught, and until the 1960s it held open-air baths with separate sections for men and women.
new.tip: The Prins Hendrikpark around the water is where the neighbourhood walks and fishes. There is a petting farm on the shore for children.

new.title: Eat at the dike brewery in Oijen
new.desc: Bierbrouwerij Oijen settled in 2002 in an old cowshed on the winter dike along the Maas, between Oijen and Macharen. The Oijens beers, from Blond and Amber to IPA and Donker, are poured in the brewery's own restaurant and on its terrace.
new.tip: It is a natural stop on a bike ride along the Maas dikes. The spot where the beer was first brewed now works as a distillery, so ask about the house spirits too.

new.title: Fill a basket at the Mariënwaerdt estate shop
new.desc: Heerlijkheid Mariënwaerdt near Beesd is an estate of some 900 hectares of fields, meadows, woods and avenues that has been in the same family since 1734. It sells its own produce in the Landgoedwinkel and runs a restaurant and the pancake house De Stapelbakker.
new.tip: The estate is open for walking and cycling, so earn your lunch with a loop along the lanes first.

new.title: Climb the wall stairs of Kasteel Ammersoyen
new.desc: Ammersoyen is a textbook medieval castle in the Bommelerwaard, with four towers, moats and a great hall six metres high. It survived a devastating fire in 1590 and a spell as a convent of Poor Clares, and a sixteen-year restoration brought back its medieval wall stairs, latrines and fireplaces.
new.tip: Do not miss the finds recovered from the moat, which show daily castle life. Opening days change with the season, so check before you go.

new.title: Step into the world of the shoe in Waalwijk
new.desc: Waalwijk grew up on shoes and leather, and its museum of the industry was founded in 1954. Since 2022 it has been called the Schoenenkwartier and fills a wing of the former town hall, with a knowledge centre and a workshop, the Schoenenlab, beside the galleries.
new.tip: Look out for workshops in the Schoenenlab if you want to make something yourself. There is a museum café for afterwards.

new.title: Read the stone carvings of Zaltbommel's Stadskasteel
new.desc: The Guelders commander Maarten van Rossum had this house built around 1535, and its turrets, battlements and rich Renaissance sculpture earned it the name city castle. Saved from demolition in 1881 and restored by Pierre Cuypers, it is now the town's history museum.
new.tip: Study the carvings on the outside before you go in. The museum has a café and a garden.

new.title: Find Kasteel Nederhemert on its island in the Maas
new.desc: Kasteel Nederhemert began shortly before 1300 as a residential tower on an island in the Maas near Heusden. It burned out in the fighting of 1944 and 1945 and stood as a ruin for decades, until a full restoration that Queen Beatrix opened in 2005.
new.tip: The castle is not a regular museum, so come for the outside and the quiet island around it. It pairs well with a visit to Heusden nearby.

new.title: Spend a beach day at the IJzeren Man in Vught
new.desc: This lake in the Vught woods was dug for sand, first for railway dikes and around 1890 to raise the Het Zand district of Den Bosch. Workers nicknamed the steam dredger the Iron Man and went on strike for fear it would take their jobs. Today there is a lakeside beach with a marked swimming area, pedal boats and mini golf.
new.tip: The beach is a summer affair, but the Strandhuys on the shore serves breakfast, lunch and dinner. The water is shallow, which suits small children.

new.title: Take the ferry to Slot Loevestein
new.desc: Loevestein was built around 1357 where the Maas and Waal meet, and later served as a state prison. Its most famous inmate, the jurist Hugo de Groot, escaped after two years hidden in a book chest. The castle and its fortress are now a museum.
new.tip: In the high season a ferry for walkers and cyclists links the castle with Woudrichem and Gorinchem, which is the nicest way to arrive.
